title: Flyby vs ZBiotics: DHM Formula vs Probiotic, Price and Stacking
excerpt: Flyby is a DHM capsule formula; ZBiotics is an engineered probiotic drink. How each works, what the evidence shows, what a night costs, and whether to stack them.
metaDescription: Flyby vs ZBiotics: a DHM capsule formula vs an engineered probiotic drink. How each works, the evidence, cost per night, and whether to take both.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** Flyby and ZBiotics are not two versions of the same thing. Flyby is a capsule supplement built around DHM (dihydromyricetin, a plant compound studied for how it interacts with alcohol in the brain and liver) plus vitamins, milk thistle, amino acids, and electrolytes. ZBiotics is a small probiotic drink made with a bacterium engineered to break down acetaldehyde, a toxic by-product of alcohol, inside your gut. Neither one has a large, independent human trial showing it prevents hangovers. If you want a pill with the better-studied main ingredient and a lower price per night, Flyby is the more sensible pick of the two. If you like the idea of one bottle before you go out and the price doesn't bother you, ZBiotics is the simpler routine. And if price is your main concern, plain DHM from a single-ingredient brand gets you Flyby's core ingredient for much less.

**The quick numbers:** at the prices we last tracked, Flyby works out to about $3.60 a serving. ZBiotics usually runs roughly $10 to $15 a bottle, depending on pack size and subscription. Plain DHM can cost under a dollar a serving. None of these replaces drinking less, eating a real meal, and drinking water between drinks.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article compares two consumer products using published research and the companies' own descriptions. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. Neither Flyby nor ZBiotics is approved by the FDA to prevent or treat hangovers, and neither one lowers your blood alcohol, sobers you up, or makes it safe to drive. **Ask a doctor or pharmacist first if** you take prescription medicine (especially anything processed by the liver, blood thinners, or sedatives), are pregnant or breastfeeding, have liver or kidney disease, or have a weakened immune system. If someone shows signs of alcohol poisoning, such as confusion, vomiting while drowsy, slow or irregular breathing, or can't be woken up, call 911.

**About our links:** we earn a commission on some DHM products on this page, including Flyby, and we say so where the links appear. We have no relationship with ZBiotics, so there are no links to buy it here.

This page is part of our Flyby comparison series. If you landed here first, our full [Flyby Recovery review](/never-hungover/flyby-recovery-review-2025) covers the product in more depth, and our [ZBiotics review](/never-hungover/zbiotics-review) does the same for the probiotic.

## Flyby vs ZBiotics at a Glance

| | Flyby Recovery | ZBiotics Pre-Alcohol Probiotic |
|---|---|---|
| Format | Capsules | Small single-serve drink |
| Main active idea | DHM plus vitamins, milk thistle, amino acids, electrolytes | Engineered *Bacillus subtilis* probiotic |
| What it targets | Alcohol's effects on the brain and liver, plus nutrient and fluid loss | Acetaldehyde made in the gut |
| When you take it | Around drinking, per the label (the brand has used a split routine: some before drinking, some before bed) | Before your first drink |
| DHM per serving | 300 mg (per the label we tracked) | None |
| Rough cost per night | About $3.60 per serving | Roughly $10 to $15 per bottle |
| Independent human evidence | Limited (DHM has more animal research than human trials) | Very limited |
| Works the morning after? | Partly designed for that, but best taken around drinking | No, it is meant to be taken before |

Prices change often and depend on pack size, retailer, and subscriptions. Treat these as a rough guide and check current pricing before you buy.

## The Core Difference: A Formula vs a Probiotic

The most useful way to compare these two is to look at what each one is actually trying to do inside your body. They aim at different parts of the same problem.

### How your body handles alcohol, in plain words

When you drink, your body breaks alcohol down in two main steps:

1. **Alcohol becomes acetaldehyde.** An enzyme called alcohol dehydrogenase turns ethanol into acetaldehyde. Acetaldehyde is toxic. It's the chemical behind the flushing, nausea, and racing heart some people get when they drink.
2. **Acetaldehyde becomes acetate.** A second enzyme, aldehyde dehydrogenase, converts acetaldehyde into acetate, which is far less harmful and eventually broken down into carbon dioxide and water.

Most of this happens in your **liver**. A smaller amount happens in your digestive tract, partly by the cells lining your gut and partly by the bacteria that already live there.

A hangover, though, is more than acetaldehyde. Researchers who study hangovers point to several contributors: the immune system's inflammatory response, poor-quality sleep after drinking, mild dehydration and lost electrolytes, low blood sugar, and congeners (other chemicals in drinks, more common in dark spirits and some wines; see our guide to [congeners in alcohol](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol)). Hangovers usually peak when blood alcohol is already near zero, which is one reason scientists still argue about how much acetaldehyde itself drives the next-day misery.

That matters for this comparison. Flyby takes a broad, multi-ingredient swing at several of those contributors. ZBiotics takes a narrow, precise swing at one of them.

### How Flyby is meant to work

Flyby Recovery is a capsule supplement. Per the label we tracked, a serving includes:

- **DHM, 300 mg.** The headline ingredient, extracted from plants such as the Japanese raisin tree (*Hovenia dulcis*) and vine tea.
- **Milk thistle.** A traditional liver herb whose main compound group is called silymarin.
- **B vitamins** (B1, B2, B6, B9, B12). Heavy drinking can deplete some B vitamins over time.
- **Vitamin C**, **apple cider vinegar**, a blend of **amino acids**, and **electrolytes** such as sodium, potassium, and magnesium.

Formulas change, so check the current label for exact amounts.

The case for DHM rests mostly on animal research. A 2012 rat study published in the *Journal of Neuroscience* (Shen and colleagues) found that DHM blunted alcohol's effects on GABA-A receptors, the brain's main calming receptors, and reduced signs of intoxication and withdrawal in the animals. Later mouse studies from the same research group suggested DHM may help the liver clear alcohol and acetaldehyde more efficiently and may reduce some alcohol-related liver stress. Human trials are small, and many test multi-ingredient products rather than DHM on its own. For a deeper look at how much DHM people take and why, see our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025).

The supporting ingredients are a mixed bag. Electrolytes and B vitamins make sense for someone who drank a lot and didn't eat or hydrate well, but they're cheap and easy to get elsewhere, and there's little direct evidence that adding them to a hangover pill changes how you feel the next day. Milk thistle has a long history of use and some research on liver health, but there's no good evidence that it prevents hangovers. The honest summary is that the DHM is doing the heavy lifting in Flyby's theory, and the rest is reasonable but lightly supported support.

### How ZBiotics is meant to work

ZBiotics makes what it calls a "pre-alcohol probiotic." The active ingredient is a strain of ***Bacillus subtilis***, a bacterium widely used in food (it's what ferments natto, a traditional Japanese soybean dish). The company genetically engineered its strain to produce an enzyme that breaks down acetaldehyde. Because *B. subtilis* forms tough spores, the company says the bacteria survive the trip through your stomach and become active in the intestines.

The idea is that some alcohol is turned into acetaldehyde in your gut, and the engineered bacteria can convert some of that to harmless acetate before it causes trouble. That's why ZBiotics tells you to drink it before your first alcoholic drink. The bacteria need to be in place while alcohol is moving through your gut. Taking it the next morning doesn't fit the mechanism.

The company is clear that ZBiotics does not lower blood alcohol or make you less drunk. It's sold as a food product, not a drug.

### Where each idea is strong and where it's weak

| | Flyby (DHM formula) | ZBiotics (engineered probiotic) |
|---|---|---|
| Strongest point | DHM has a bigger body of published research, including brain and liver studies | A precise, clever mechanism with lab evidence that the strain makes the enzyme |
| Biggest open question | Most DHM data is from animals; human trials are small and mostly test blends | Most acetaldehyde is made in the liver, not the gut, so the gut-only effect may be small |
| What it does not do | Doesn't make heavy drinking safe or lower blood alcohol | Doesn't lower blood alcohol or touch acetaldehyde made in the liver |
| Extra ingredients | Several, each lightly supported for hangovers | None to speak of |

## What the Evidence Actually Says

This is the section that matters most, and it's where both products have to be judged honestly.

**For Flyby**, the evidence is really evidence about DHM, plus general knowledge about the supporting ingredients. We don't know of a published, independent clinical trial of Flyby Recovery itself. DHM's research base is genuinely interesting, but it leans heavily on rodents and cell studies. A mouse that drinks less or recovers faster is a useful signal, not proof that a 300 mg capsule will change your Sunday morning.

**For ZBiotics**, the company has shared results from its own testing, and lab work shows the engineered strain does what it was built to do: produce the enzyme and break down acetaldehyde. As of this writing, we haven't found a large, independent, peer-reviewed human trial showing that ZBiotics reduces hangover symptoms. The unresolved scientific issue is simple to state. If most acetaldehyde is produced and handled in the liver, then a probiotic working only in the gut can only touch a slice of the total. How big and how meaningful that slice is for how you feel the next day hasn't been settled.

Put side by side, **DHM has more published research behind it than ZBiotics' engineered strain**, and neither product has the kind of independent human data you'd want before calling it proven. That's not a knock on either company. It's the state of hangover research in general, which is a small and underfunded field.

### What real users tend to say

User sentiment for both products is mixed in a similar way, and it's worth summarizing fairly:

- **Flyby** has thousands of customer reviews on Amazon with a generally positive average. People who like it often say it takes the edge off a moderate night, especially headaches and that drained feeling. Common complaints are the price compared with plain DHM, the number of capsules per serving, capsule size, and that it doesn't do much after a truly heavy night.
- **ZBiotics** has loyal fans who say they notice a real difference, especially with flushing or a queasy stomach. On forums like Reddit you'll also find plenty of people who say they couldn't tell any difference, and the cost per bottle comes up again and again. Some reviewers point out that it's hard to judge, because people who take it tend to also hydrate and pace themselves more carefully on those nights.

That last point applies to both products. Customer reviews can't separate the supplement's effect from the placebo effect, from drinking less that night, or from simply having a good night's sleep. They tell you how satisfied buyers are, not whether the product works.

## Price Math: What a Night Actually Costs

Price is where these two separate most clearly. Here's the math using the prices we last tracked. Your numbers will vary.

| Option | Typical cost per serving | 4 nights a month | 8 nights a month |
|---|---|---|---|
| Flyby Recovery | About $3.60 | About $14.50 | About $29 |
| ZBiotics | Roughly $10 to $15 | Roughly $40 to $60 | Roughly $80 to $120 |
| Flyby + ZBiotics together | Roughly $14 to $19 | Roughly $55 to $75 | Roughly $110 to $150 |
| Plain DHM (single-ingredient) | Often $0.50 to $0.80 | About $2 to $3 | About $4 to $7 |

A few things to keep in mind:

- **Flyby's price depends heavily on pack size.** Small packs cost more per serving. Larger packs and sales can bring the per-serving price down.
- **ZBiotics is cheapest with bulk packs and subscriptions**, but even at its lowest it costs several times more per night than Flyby.
- **Heavier nights don't change ZBiotics' cost** since it's one bottle per night, while some DHM users take more on a bigger night. Check the label rather than assuming more is better.
- **Over a year, the gap is real.** At eight nights a month, the difference between Flyby and ZBiotics is roughly $600 to $1,000 a year, and the difference between ZBiotics and plain DHM is larger still.

If you're paying for a product with limited human evidence either way, it's reasonable to start with the cheaper one and see whether it does anything for you before spending more.

## Can You Take Flyby and ZBiotics Together?

Yes, in principle. Because they work in different places and in different ways, there's no obvious reason they would clash. ZBiotics acts in the gut on acetaldehyde, and Flyby's DHM is thought to act mainly in the brain and liver. People who stack them usually drink the ZBiotics bottle before their first drink and take Flyby per its label around the night.

A few honest caveats before you stack:

- **Nobody has studied the combination.** "These shouldn't interfere" isn't the same as "together they work better." There's no published data on stacking them.
- **You double the cost and the uncertainty.** Stacking puts you at roughly $14 to $19 a night for two products that each lack strong human evidence.
- **Supplements can still interact with medicines.** DHM and milk thistle are processed by the liver, and there's limited data on how they interact with prescription drugs. If you take any regular medication, ask a pharmacist before adding either product, let alone both. Our [DHM medication interactions guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers what's known.
- **A stack can make heavy drinking feel safer than it is.** Neither product lowers blood alcohol, protects you from alcohol poisoning, or makes it safe to drive. Feeling less rough the next morning isn't the same as your body having taken less damage.

If you want to experiment, a more useful approach than stacking from day one is to try one product for a few nights, then the other, keeping what you drink roughly the same. That tells you more about what actually helps you than taking both at once.

## Which One Should You Choose?

There's no winner that fits everyone, but there are clear fits for different people.

**Flyby is the better fit if you:**

- Want the ingredient with more published research behind it (DHM)
- Prefer capsules to a drink
- Want something you can take partly later in the night or before bed
- Care about cost per night and drink fairly often
- Like the idea of electrolytes and B vitamins in the same product

**ZBiotics is the better fit if you:**

- Want a single bottle before you go out and nothing else to remember
- Are specifically curious about the gut acetaldehyde idea
- Don't drink often, so the cost per night matters less
- Would rather not take a DHM product for some reason, such as a medication concern your doctor raised

**Neither is a great fit if you:**

- Are hoping to drink more without consequences. Nothing in a bottle does that.
- Have liver disease, are pregnant, or take medicines that interact with alcohol. Talk to your doctor first.
- Get severe or worsening hangovers. That can be a sign you're drinking more than your body handles well, and it's worth talking to a doctor about.

### Where plain DHM fits in

Flyby's main ingredient is DHM. If that's what you're mostly paying for, a single-ingredient DHM supplement gets you more DHM per serving for much less money. You give up the vitamins, milk thistle, and electrolytes, which you can get from food, a sports drink, or a basic multivitamin anyway.

Our [Flyby vs Double Wood comparison](/never-hungover/flyby-vs-double-wood-complete-comparison-2025) goes through that trade-off in detail. In short:

- **[Flyby Recovery on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0CCK34H46?tag=dhmguide-20)** (affiliate link): about $3.60 a serving at the price we tracked, with 300 mg DHM plus the supporting blend.
- **[Double Wood DHM on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20)** (affiliate link): 1,000 mg DHM per serving at around $0.80 a serving at the price we tracked.
- **[NusaPure DHM on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B08B32XBRB?tag=dhmguide-20)** (affiliate link): 1,000 mg DHM at around $0.50 a serving at the price we tracked.

## How Flyby vs ZBiotics Compares to the Rest of the Series

We've compared Flyby against several other hangover brands. The pattern is consistent: Flyby sits in the middle on price, uses a moderate DHM dose with a lot of supporting ingredients, and is clear about how much DHM it contains. Against ZBiotics, the comparison is less about dose and more about two entirely different approaches.

- [Flyby vs Cheers](/never-hungover/flyby-vs-cheers-complete-comparison-2025) compares two DHM-based formulas head to head.
- [ZBiotics vs Cheers](/never-hungover/zbiotics-vs-cheers) is the closest sibling to this page, comparing the probiotic against another DHM brand.
- [DHM vs ZBiotics](/never-hungover/dhm-vs-zbiotics) compares the probiotic against DHM as an ingredient rather than any single brand.

## What Actually Helps a Hangover Most

Whatever you choose, the basics do more than any supplement:

1. **Drink less, or pace yourself.** The single most reliable way to have a smaller hangover is to drink less alcohol. Alternating each drink with a glass of water helps you do that naturally.
2. **Eat before and while you drink.** Food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol enters your blood.
3. **Choose lighter drinks when you can.** Clear spirits tend to contain fewer congeners than dark ones, and some people find red wine hits them harder.
4. **Protect your sleep.** Alcohol disrupts sleep quality, and poor sleep makes everything the next day feel worse.
5. **Rehydrate in the morning** with water or an electrolyte drink, and eat something gentle.

Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) goes through each of these in more detail, and our upcoming guide to [what to take before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-take-before-drinking) compares the main pre-drinking options side by side.

### A note on painkillers

Some people reach for a painkiller alongside a hangover supplement. Be careful here. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) is processed by the liver, and regular heavy drinking raises the risk of liver damage from it; our guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains the safe limits. Anti-inflammatory painkillers like ibuprofen can irritate a stomach that alcohol has already irritated. Read the label, take a standard dose with food, and ask a pharmacist if you're unsure.

## The Bottom Line

Flyby and ZBiotics are both legitimate products from real companies, and neither one is a scam. They're also both premium-priced for products without strong independent human evidence. Flyby's main ingredient, DHM, has the larger body of published research, mostly from animal studies, and it costs a fraction of ZBiotics per night. ZBiotics has a novel and genuinely clever mechanism, but it can only act on the share of acetaldehyde made in your gut, and its human evidence comes mainly from the company itself.

If you're choosing between the two, Flyby is the more reasonable starting point for most people on cost and evidence. If you mainly want DHM, a single-ingredient DHM supplement is cheaper still. If you're curious about ZBiotics and the price doesn't bother you, it's a fair experiment. Stacking them is possible but unstudied, and it doubles what you spend. And none of them replaces drinking less, eating, drinking water, and getting some sleep.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is Flyby or ZBiotics better for hangovers?**

Neither has strong independent human evidence, so there's no proven winner. Flyby's main ingredient, DHM, has more published research behind it, mostly in animals, and it costs about $3.60 a serving versus roughly $10 to $15 for a ZBiotics bottle. ZBiotics uses an engineered probiotic that breaks down acetaldehyde in the gut, a clever but narrower approach. For most people, Flyby is the more sensible starting point on cost and evidence.

**Can I take Flyby and ZBiotics together?**

There's no known reason they would interfere with each other, since they work in different places: ZBiotics in the gut and DHM mainly in the brain and liver. But nobody has studied the combination, so there's no evidence that stacking works better than either alone, and it costs far more than Flyby alone. If you take prescription medicine, ask a pharmacist first.

**What is the difference between Flyby and ZBiotics?**

Flyby is a capsule supplement built around 300 mg of DHM plus milk thistle, B vitamins, vitamin C, amino acids, and electrolytes. ZBiotics is a probiotic drink containing a *Bacillus subtilis* strain engineered to produce an enzyme that breaks down acetaldehyde, a toxic by-product of alcohol, in your gut. Flyby takes a broad, multi-ingredient approach, while ZBiotics targets one step in how the body handles alcohol.

**Does ZBiotics or Flyby lower your blood alcohol?**

No. Neither product lowers blood alcohol, makes you less drunk, or speeds up how fast you sober up. ZBiotics says this clearly itself. Don't use either product as a reason to drink more or to drive after drinking.

**Can I take Flyby or ZBiotics the morning after drinking?**

ZBiotics is designed to be taken before your first drink, so taking it the next morning doesn't fit how it's meant to work. Flyby's label has used a routine that includes a dose later in the night or before bed, but like most DHM products it's intended to be taken around drinking rather than as a next-day cure. The next morning, water, electrolytes, food, and rest are your best tools.

**Is Flyby or ZBiotics safe?**

Both are generally considered safe for healthy adults when used as labeled. *Bacillus subtilis* is widely used in food, and DHM has been well tolerated in the limited human research available. Ask a doctor or pharmacist first if you take prescription medicine, have liver disease, are pregnant or breastfeeding, or have a weakened immune system. Neither product makes heavy drinking safe.

**Is ZBiotics worth the money compared with Flyby?**

It depends on how often you drink and how much the price matters to you. At roughly $10 to $15 a bottle, ZBiotics costs several times more per night than Flyby, and its human evidence comes mainly from the company. If you drink a few times a month and are curious, it's a reasonable experiment. If you drink more often or want the ingredient with more research behind it, Flyby or a plain DHM supplement is better value.

**Is there a cheaper alternative to both?**

Yes. Single-ingredient DHM supplements often cost under $1 a serving and contain more DHM per serving than Flyby. You give up the extra vitamins and electrolytes, which you can get from food, a sports drink, or a basic multivitamin. You can also skip supplements entirely: drinking less, eating, and alternating drinks with water make the biggest difference.
